transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what finally made me come in is that I feel like I’m always in motion, even when there’s no real reason to be. I don’t mean I’m doing anything dramatic, but on a quiet day at home I’ll be up and down, moving from one thing to the next. I’ll start looking over the garden club list, then suddenly I’m over by my knitting bag sorting that out, and before I’ve really finished either of those I’m pulling out travel papers or checking something else.

It’s like I don’t settle into one thing properly. I keep thinking, “Oh, I should just take care of this,” and then another thing catches my attention, and I’m off again. It makes me feel a bit scattered, I guess, and tired of myself sometimes. Even when I’m supposed to be having a quiet day, I don’t really feel quiet inside.
Do you ever have times when your mood feels unusually high or overly cheerful for you?

Hmm… unusually high? I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I have days where I’m in a decent mood, of course, or I get pleased about something—like if the garden club plans come together or I’ve had a nice call with someone—but I don’t think of myself as being overly cheerful in a way that feels unlike me.

I suppose I can get a little keyed up if there’s something to look forward to, but I’m not sure that’s what you mean. It’s more ordinary excitement, I think, not some big shift where I feel on top of the world or anything like that.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even about everyday things?

I’m not sure I’d say I worry a lot, exactly. I mean, I do think about everyday things—probably more than I need to sometimes—but I don’t know that it feels like worry in the way you might mean.

Like, I might go over whether I’ve remembered something or whether I should take care of some little task, but it’s not always that I’m afraid something terrible will happen. It’s more that things sit in my mind and I keep circling back to them. But no, I don’t think I’m someone who’s constantly worrying about everything, at least not that I’ve noticed.
Do unwanted thoughts keep popping into your mind even when you try not to think about them?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re describing, I don’t believe. I mean, thoughts pop into my head all the time, but I wouldn’t say they’re unwanted thoughts that frighten me or that I’m fighting to keep out.

Sometimes I’ll remember something I meant to do, or I’ll suddenly think, “Oh, did I put that away?” or “I should check on that,” but that feels more like my mind wandering or jumping around than a thought intruding on me. I don’t usually have a particular thought that keeps forcing its way in when I’m trying not to think about it.

I may be misunderstanding what you mean, though. If you mean upsetting thoughts that won’t leave me alone, no, I haven’t really noticed that.
Have you had trouble paying attention since you were a child?

Yes, I think so. Looking back, it really did start when I was little, though of course at the time nobody talked about it the way people do now.

In grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother I was bright, but scattered — that was the word that seemed to follow me around. I’d lose papers, forget to turn things in, or have them somewhere in my desk all crumpled up. And I remember getting in trouble for talking out of turn, not because I was trying to be rude, I just had something in my head and it would come out before I’d really thought about it.

I also had a hard time sitting still long enough to finish my work. I’d be wiggling in my seat or fussing with things, and then the work wouldn’t get done even though I understood it. So yes, I’d say the paying attention trouble was there even back then.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with childhood-onset inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. The patient describes lifelong distractibility, difficulty sustaining focus, shifting between tasks, inner restlessness, losing papers, forgetting to turn in work, blurting out answers, and difficulty sitting still since grade school.
